To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a method for regression verification that is based on the following steps: (1) the generation of a set of test cases that covers all possible executions of the original program, (2) the construction of the original program’s transition system, (3) the construction of a transition system of the new program, and (4) the verification that the new program is a refinement of the original program.
we developed a method for verifying that a new revision does not break existing behavior of a PLC program and that we implemented this method in the toolset RegVer.
we have developed a novel regression verification method for PLC code, and that this method is applicable in practice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: Given two revisions A and B of a PLC program, can we prove that the behavior of B is a superset of A?

the following question: Given a set of test cases, which represent the intended behavior of the plant’s PLC software, can one automatically prove that a new version of the software does not break any of the intended behaviors?
the problem of verifying the correctness of PLC code in a way that is both efficient and applicable to large PLC code bases in industrial settings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

The method presented in this paper allows to prove that the new software revision does not introduce new faults in the plant’s behavior, and that the new software does not remove any existing faults in the plant's behavior.

a regression verification of the new PLC software revision with the help of the presented method would prove that this new revision is a correct implementation of the original requirements, and does not introduce unintended behavior in comparison to the previous software revision.
a new version of the software is correct, i.e. it does not contain errors, and it does not change the behavior of the system, i.e. the new version does not introduce any new errors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presented method is a first step towards a formal approach for the verification of PLC code.
we have shown that it is possible to verify the correctness of a new PLC software revision with respect to a given reference model.
we have shown that it is feasible to verify a PLC program with the help of a formal model checker.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the verification problem is tractable and that our approach scales to realistic examples.
the verification problem for PLC code is a lot more tractable than previously believed.
it is possible to verify a large PLC program (more than 200,000 lines of code), which is a major improvement compared to the state of the art.
